evidence_quotes.quote: Persistent disparities in access to water and sanitation services in HICs cannot be explained by an absence of resources or capacity, but are driven by environmental discrimination, systemic racism, and social exclusion.

The linking of property to water and sanitation services is a policy choice that disadvantages migrant populations, including nomadic populations, displaced people, people experiencing homelessness or in unstable housing, people living in poverty in rural areas, people who are incarcerated, and people without access to housing with functioning indoor plumbing.

We also included key reports, government documents, and UN resolutions where these directly inform our analysis. Our Review is also informed by our collective experiences in working with underserved communities in high-income countries.
Until May, 2020, Irongate’s residents did not have access to the municipal water and sanitation services provided to the white neighbourhood across the road, which was part of Apex.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to drinking water and sanitation services across marginalised groups in high-income countries.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading: under the plain wording, it examines legal, regulatory, institutional, and governance factors shaping WASH disparities; under the narrow rule-type reading, it specifically discusses rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access, including municipal incorporation/underbounding boundaries, full-cost recovery tariff structures and disconnection for non-payment, linking service provision to property ownership/tenure, and criminalisation of open defecation and septic non-compliance.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). Although published as a Lancet Global Health Review with a brief search-strategy box, it presents no primary empirical data and is not a systematic empirical synthesis (no eligibility screening protocol, study selection counts, systematic data extraction, quality appraisal, or structured synthesis, explicitly drawing on selected reports, resolutions, and the authors' collective experiences to provide a thematic narrative and policy overview).
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses relevant service-access outcomes—including lack of municipal water/sewer connections, intermittent supply, affordability, involuntary water shutoffs, and reliance on public toilets or wells—via secondary literature and short illustrative text panels, though without primary or systematically synthesized outcome data.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifiable as a narrative policy/thematic review, but lacks an empirical study population/sample, analytical unit of analysis, or systematic review study-selection structure linking a defined exposure to measured outcomes.

country: High-income countries (illustrative examples from USA, France, Italy, Slovakia, UK, Australia, Canada, Greece, and South Korea)
population_and_sample: Marginalised populations in high-income countries (narrative overview; no primary sample or systematic review study sample reported)
exposure: Systemic racism, social exclusion, municipal underbounding, full-cost recovery tariffs, and linking water and sanitation service provision to property ownership
outcome: Household and community drinking water and sanitation access, municipal connection, affordability, and involuntary water shutoffs (cited from secondary literature)
rationale: Although this Lancet Global Health Review directly addresses household and community water and sanitation access (c1) and discusses rule-type legal, regulatory, and tariff/tenure mechanisms governing access under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2 (c2), it is a thematic narrative and policy review rather than an original empirical study or a systematic empirical synthesis (c3 = no). It collects no primary data and applies no systematic screening, extraction, or synthesis methodology, relying on illustrative secondary examples and the authors' collective experiences. Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence).
